title: COMPLLLM: Fine-tuning LLMs to Discover Complementary Signals for Decision-making
claim: Prior methods target only concepts in one source or signals predictive of the target; ours targets information that also complements an existing recommendation.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, Venn diagrams with hatched target region
description: Three side-by-side Venn-style diagrams on a white background, each captioned in bold below. The left, "Identifying concepts", has a green "Text" circle filled with a checkered pattern, with two faint dashed gray circles behind it. The middle, "Identifying signals", shows overlapping green "Text" and blue "State" circles, where only their intersection is checkered, with a faint dashed gray circle below. The right, "Identifying complementary signals", shows green Text, blue State and an orange "Recommendation" circle, all solid. Only the Text∩State region outside the Recommendation circle is filled with diagonal stripes. The eye goes to the stripes in the right panel, which mark the target of each method. The progression adds one more circle each time.
caption: A graphical representation of how our work goes beyond simply identifying concepts that appear in text or signals that are predictive of a target state, by also ensuring that signals complement the existing recommendation. The diagonal stripes (twill pattern) represent the target of the corresponding methods.
abstract: Multi-agent decision pipelines can outperform single agent workflows when complementarity holds, i.e., different agents bring unique information to inform a final decision. We propose ComplLLM, a post-training framework based on decision theory that fine-tunes a decision-assistant LLM to output signals that complement existing agent decisions, using complementary information as reward. We validate ComplLLM on synthetic and real-world tasks involving domain experts, demonstrating how the approach recovers known complementary information, produces plausible explanations of complementary signals to support downstream decision-makers, and improves human and LLM agent decision performance in controlled studies.
